blurb: Honda CB750: the bike that invented the superbike for everyone. Disc brake, four pipes, and a whole industry scrambling to catch up. Proper foundation myth.

characteristics.signature: the performance king that raised the bar

blurb: Kawasaki Z1: after the CB750, Kawasaki said 'hold my wrench' and dropped a 900 that owned the seventies. Legend status, earned.
Ducati 900SS: lean, loud, and desmo through and through. The shape of Italian race DNA before the 916 made it a poster. Respect.
Suzuki GSX-R750: the original race-replica that taught the world what a street superbike should feel like. Slabside to SRAD — pure Gixxer religion.
Honda RC30: homologation royalty. Expensive then, priceless now, and still the bike people lower their voice to talk about. Elite taste.
Honda Fireblade: Tadao Baba's lightweight revolution. Not the most horsepower — just the most important. The Blade that cut the rulebook.

characteristics.signature: the shape that made everyone else look ordinary

blurb: Ducati 916: Tamburini sculpture with Fogarty WSBK DNA. Underseat exhausts, single-sider, and a silhouette still stealing the show. Iconic doesn't cover it.

characteristics.signature: redefined what a litre bike should be

blurb: Yamaha R1: that crossplane howl and the feeling the front end is reading your mind. From '98 on, the litre class had a new boss.
Suzuki Hayabusa: the bird of prey that made speedometers blush. Controversially shaped, cultishly loved. Gen-1 copper still starts arguments.
Honda SP-1 / SP-2: WSBK twin that punched Ducati in the badge. Race-rep paint jobs still haunt paddocks. Proper hero bike.
Suzuki GSX-R1000: especially the early K1 era — the litre race-rep that owned the 2000s. Light, vicious, and still grinned about in sheds.
Kawasaki ZX-10R: green meanie. WSBK has a lot to thank this bike for. If you love the Ninja, you love winning.

characteristics.signature: when BMW decided to build a superbike

blurb: BMW S1000RR: asymmetric headlights and serious power. The Germans decided to build a superbike. They succeeded.
Kawasaki Ninja H2: supercharged insanity in street clothes. When magazines need a cover bike that breaks brains, this is it.
Norton Manx: Featherbed frame, Isle of Man lore, and the sound of a single that built British racing. Hailwood's playground. Pure icon.
Norton Commando: Isolastic twin attitude when Japan was inventing the superbike. Fastback, Roadster, Yellow Peril — British character on two wheels.

characteristics.signature: NZ garage genius that beat the factories

blurb: Britten V1000: built in a New Zealand workshop, carbon-fibre bones, and faster thinking than the factory teams. Only a handful exist — dream-bike royalty.

characteristics.signature: sounds like an argument and goes like a missile

blurb: Ducati Panigale V4: the bike that sounds like an argument and goes like a missile. You don't choose the Panigale life — it chooses you.

characteristics.signature: Italian twin with manners and menace

blurb: Ducati Panigale V2: twin-cylinder Italian attitude without needing a factory contract. Beautiful, sharp, and still very Ducati.
Aprilia RSV4: V4 symphony and Italian attitude. If you picked Aprilia, you don't do boring. We approve.
Aprilia Tuono: superbike heart with the fairings thrown away. Wheelie-friendly Italian chaos. Excellent life choice.
Aprilia RSV Mille: Noale's V-twin that proved Aprilia belonged with the big boys. 90s/00s cult classic. Nice deep cut.
MV Agusta F4: Tamburini art with a four-exhaust symphony. They don't make many, and they don't need to. Rare taste.

characteristics.signature: Italian sculpture that happens to go fast

blurb: MV Agusta: art on two wheels. Brutale, Dragster, or F4 — you've got rare taste and you know it.
Honda CBR1000RR Fireblade: HRC DNA in a road bike. Decades of Blade lineage and still cutting corners with class.
Honda RC213V-S: as close as most mortals get to a MotoGP bike with number plates. Exotic doesn't begin to cover it.
Triumph Speed Triple: that triple soundtrack and streetfighter stare. British character with enough torque to make corners optional.
Triumph Street Triple: the middleweight grin machine. Light, loud enough, and always up for another corner.
Triumph Daytona 675: the triple that made supersport interesting again. Soundtrack alone is worth the price of admission.
KTM Super Duke: orange, unapologetic, and ready to misbehave. You clearly like a bit of chaos.
KTM RC8: Austria's V-twin superbike statement. Rare, angular, and very orange. Cult pick.
Yamaha R6: the supersport scalpel. High-revving, track-day royalty, and still the bike that teaches corner speed properly.
Kawasaki ZX-6R / 636: middleweight Ninja bite. Track-day favourite with proper green menace. Solid choice.
Honda CBR600RR: the complete middleweight. Balanced, sharp, and still the reference for 'just ride it faster.'
Suzuki GSX-R600: flickable Gixxer energy in supersport form. Light, honest, and still making riders grin.
Yamaha R3: the gateway drug done right. Light, friendly, and still enough fun to remind you why you started.
Kawasaki Ninja 400: small bike, big grin. Track days, learner plates, and more fun per cc than the brochure admits.
KTM RC 390: orange pocket rocket. Sharp enough to teach race lines without needing a second mortgage.
Honda RC45: the RC30's fiercer little sibling. Homologation special energy and V4 howl. Deep-cut excellence.
Kawasaki ZX-7R: 90s green superbike icon. Twin-headlight stare and club-racing immortality. Proper nostalgia pick.

characteristics.signature: the big Ninja before the ZX-10R

blurb: Kawasaki ZX-9R: the big Ninja before the ZX-10R took over. Torque, drama, and 90s/00s streetfighter dreams.
Yamaha FZR1000: Genesis motor, EXUP valve, and the muscle that led toward the R1. 80s/90s Yamaha done loud.

characteristics.signature: the naked that started a category

blurb: Ducati Monster: the naked that spawned a thousand streetfighters. Trellis, desmo, and café attitude. Timeless.
Yamaha RD350/400: two-stroke cult classic. The smell, the scream, the stories. If this is your favourite, you know.
Kawasaki Mach H1/H2: two-stroke triple chaos from an era before traction control. Wild, smoky, unforgettable.
Triumph Bonneville: the British icon. Café racers, desert sleds, and a name that still means motorcycle. Classic taste.
Laverda Jota: Italian triple thunder with a cult following. Rare, loud, and never boring. Excellent deep cut.
Bimota: Rimini exotica — chassis jewellery wrapped around serious engines. Magazine dream-bike energy. Rare taste confirmed.

characteristics.signature: the Desmoquattro that started the modern Ducati SBK story

blurb: Ducati 851/888: Desmoquattro beginnings of modern Ducati WSBK dominance. Before the 916 — the spark. Proper history.
